- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly, especially after sharp spikes.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates; adjust upward slightly to avoid premature bottoming.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior day), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; cap forecast at 1–2% below peak or use moving average to dampen momentum.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa), model lags by 1–3 days; apply a 1–2 day lag correction or use sentiment-weighted smoothing.
- If model forecast is flat or trending upward while sentiment is negative, reduce forecast slope; avoid “false optimism” in low-sentiment periods.
- In low-sentiment environments (sentiment <0.33 for 3+ days), model often undercorrects; add 0.5–1.5% upward bias to account for mean reversion toward mid-range.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 50% of 30d average), model tends to ignore it; apply a 1–3 day smoothing filter or use sentiment-adjusted moving average.
